---
title: "Preprocessing, imputation and coverage"
---

## Preprocessing, imputation, missing features

### The input contract

Rows are samples, columns are features. Feature names are the identifiers the clock coefficients
use: `cg00000029` for methylation probes, and the declared analyte names for clinical chemistry and
NMR. `fa.FalconData` holds the matrix in `X`, sample metadata (age, sex, tissue, group) in `obs`,
and per-feature annotation in `var`; it reads and writes AnnData's `.h5ad`.

### EPIC v2 probe aggregation

EPIC v2 column names look like `cg00000029_TC21`. `fa.prepare()` strips the suffix and averages
replicate probes of the same CpG before anything else. Skipping this means every clock sees almost
no overlapping features on EPIC v2 data.

### Two distinct imputation stages

**Stage 1 - dataset-level, before the clock.** `fa.preprocess.impute()` with `median` (default),
`mean` or `none`, run only when asked.

**Stage 2 - clock-level, for features the dataset does not contain at all.** Filling with zero
in beta space means "fully unmethylated", which is biologically wrong for most sites, so FALCONAge
never does it.

**What FALCONAge does, and what the R packages do.** For a linear clock FALCONAge fills an absent
feature with the mean of the clock's observed features over the whole dataset: one constant, the
same for every absent feature and every sample (`models/linear.py`). `imputation="reference"`
replaces it with a per-feature value wherever a reference is supplied. The mitotic mean,
percentile and transmission clocks (epiTOC1/2/3, HypoClock, EPICmitHyper/Hypo, stemTOC,
stemTOCvitro) are the exception: their published statistic is taken over the sites present, so
FALCONAge leaves absent sites out and records `imputation: "excluded"`. methylclock 1.16.0 leaves
absent CpGs out of the sum (`predAge` in `R/internals.R`), which is a fill of 0. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0
fills each one with its per-probe mean from the package's `golden_ref` table (`meanImputation`,
called from `methyAge`). Each policy adds the same amount to every sample, so on one dataset the
packages differ by a constant

```
Δ = Σ_{j absent} w_j (f_j − g_j)
```

where `w_j` is the coefficient and `f_j`, `g_j` are the two fills. For Horvath's clocks the
constant is multiplied by 21 above the adult age of 20, where the anti-log transform is linear.

On a dataset that lacks some of a clock's CpGs, the packages in circulation fill them
differently (methylclock and dnaMethyAge among them), and that alone can move the same clock's age
by several years between packages that agree on every coefficient and intercept. Given identical
complete input there is no difference to explain: the conformance suite in `test/conformance/`
scores 75 clock-package pairs on the same filled matrix, and every difference left over is traced
to a coefficient copy that departs from its primary source. The offsets belong to a dataset's missing CpGs, not to the clocks, so the registry does not carry
them as per-clock discrepancies. The coverage record (`res.coverage[clock_id]`) gives the number
of values filled (`n_imputed`) and the method (`imputation`). Neither 0 nor a pooled mean is a published value for a CpG, which is why a
per-CpG reference from each clock's own training data is the better fill.

**Horvath's normalisation is optional in his own code, and the packages default differently.**
Horvath 2013 supplied a calibration step (Additional file 24, `BMIQcalibration`): each sample's
betas over 21,368 probes are mapped onto the distribution of `goldstandard2`, the per-probe means
in Additional file 22 ([Genome Biology, CC BY 2.0](https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2013-14-10-r115)),
after absent probes are set to those means. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 runs it by default for
`HorvathS2013` (`simple_mode = TRUE` skips it), methylclock 1.16.0 does not (`normalize = FALSE`),
and FALCONAge offers it as an opt-in step, `fa.preprocess.horvath_normalise()` (R:
`horvath_normalise()`). The step mostly moves the level of Horvath 2013 age rather than the
ranking of samples, so a comparison across packages has to say whether it ran.

`horvath_normalise()` is a port of `BMIQcalibration`. The R code fits its beta mixtures on
20,000 probes drawn by `set.seed(1); sample(...)` and stops its optimisers early (Nelder-Mead
after 50 evaluations), so its result depends on the exact draw and the exact optimiser path; the
port reproduces each piece as R computes it (the Mersenne-Twister draw, `optim`'s Nelder-Mead
and BFGS, RPMM's `blc`, `density()`). Against the unmodified Additional file 24 it agrees to
3e-10 in beta on a synthetic fixture and to 2e-8 years of Horvath age on the 120 samples above,
reproducing the −1.87-year shift. Two arguments follow the code people actually ran:

| Argument | Default | The other value |
|---|---|---|
| `absent` | `"drop"`: calibrate on the gold-standard probes the data carry, as Knight et al.'s published wrapper does | `"fill"`: set absent probes to their gold-standard value first |
| `sample_kind` | `"Rejection"`: R 3.6.0 and later | `"Rounding"`: the draw of earlier R |

With `sample_kind="Rounding"`, Knight et al.'s own test dataset gives 37.3665, 38.3463 and
39.322 weeks against the 37.366, 38.346 and 39.324 their instructions state; the remaining 0.002
is their k-nearest-neighbour imputation of 51 missing values. Only the 21,368 gold-standard probes
are changed, and a missing value is set to its gold-standard value first, as Horvath's code does
for a single sample; both counts are recorded in `uns["horvath_normalisation"]`.

Reporting the imputation method alongside a score is not optional; it changes the answer, and
the run manifest records it.

### Preprocessing steps that live inside a model

These are per-clock and must run *after* feature selection, not before:

| Step | Clocks in the catalogue |
|---|---|
| robust scale `(x − median)/std` | AltumAge |
| per-sample z-score across features | ZhangEN, ZhangBLUP |
| mean over non-missing | epiTOC1, HypoClock, EPICmitHyper, EPICmitHypo |
| 0.95 quantile over non-missing | stemTOC, stemTOCvitro |
| nan → 0 | epiTOC2, epiTOC3 |
| NaN → reference value | most linear clocks |

## Platform coverage
Worth running once on an array you have not used before. It reports, per clock, how many features
are present **and** how much of the model's weight they carry. Two different numbers, and the
second is the one that catches EPIC v2 probe loss:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
fa.probe_loss(d, clocks="scoreable")
```

### R

```r
probe_loss(d, clocks = "scoreable")
```

:::

::: {.falcon-output}
```
                   tier  n_features  n_present  coverage  mass_coverage  bias_years          heaviest_absent
horvath2013     bundled         353        339    0.9603         0.9715     -1.2570   cg11932564 (0.8%), ...
hannum          bundled          71         64    0.9014         0.8994      1.0279   cg21139312 (2.7%), ...
zhangmortality  bundled          10          9    0.9000         0.7687      0.0124  cg08362785 (23.1%), ...
```
:::

Three rows of the table for the EPIC v2 series in the test corpus (GSE330325). `zhangmortality`
has nine of its ten CpGs, 90% by count, and the one it lacks carries 23% of its weight.

`bias_years` is filled in when the platform is one the shift has been measured on; see
[what probe loss costs](../methods/uncertainty.qmd#probe-loss-priced). `NaN` there means *not measured*, never
*no bias*.

A clock at 96% feature coverage and 61% weight coverage has kept nearly all its probes and lost
the ones that matter. The scoring floor applies to both measures, so this run would be refused
with a message naming the heaviest absent probes rather than returning a confident number.
